title: Oankar close
hook: a poem made of a scholar's own alphabet, sung back to him as an invitation: closing the Oankar with humble learning

segments.voice: Yesterday, writing on the forehead: the record a life writes, and the grace that can arrive. Your line was what's written. Did the good deed you chose get finished? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-three.

Who explains things best? Often not the one who knows the most. It's the one who remembers what it was like not to know. The patient older cousin. The coworker who says, I got this wrong for years, here's what finally helped. For a week now this path has been reading the Oankar, Guru Nanak's long alphabet poem in Raga Ramkali, spoken to a pandit, a teacher of letters. Today we close it. And the question for the close is not what the poem knows. It's how it teaches.
screen: `THE ONE WHO REMEMBERS NOT KNOWING.` → `A WEEK IN THE OANKAR.` → `NOT WHAT IT KNOWS. HOW IT TEACHES.`

segments.voice: First, look back at what we walked through. The poem opens with Oankar, the One, from whom even Brahma came. We heard it ask whether the pandit has understood what he reads. We stood with it on a riverbank where a tree can fall at any time. We heard that true learning is reflection on the Name, and yesterday, that a record is being written. Second, notice who it's spoken to. Its center line, the Rahao, says, in paraphrase: listen, pandit, why write about the world's tangles? Write the Name of the Lord, as one who faces the Guru. Listen. It doesn't mock the teacher or tell him to burn his books. It leaves the letters on his board where they are, and asks them to carry the Name. That's an invitation, not a defeat. Third, look at how Guru Nanak speaks of himself elsewhere. In the Japji, on ang four, after a long list of the world's foolishness and cruelty, he signs the stanza, in paraphrase: lowly Nanak offers this reflection. The one bringing a new reading of the alphabet doesn't stand above the learner. He sits beside him and calls himself small. Fourth, put the two together. The Oankar teaches humility to the learned, and it teaches humbly. Both halves matter. Knowledge that looks down on people has missed the poem's point. Knowledge that kneels beside someone and says, here, look at this letter with me, has caught it. That's how the Oankar closes for us: an alphabet that asks a teacher to listen, and a teacher who calls himself lowly. Today's line: humble learning.
screen: `A WEEK IN THE OANKAR.` · `LISTEN, PANDIT: AN INVITATION.` · `LOWLY NANAK OFFERS THIS.` · `HUMILITY, TAUGHT HUMBLY.` · then, large: `HUMBLE LEARNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to teach one thing humbly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you know well: a recipe, a tool, a song, a shortcut at work, a line from scripture. Now think of one person who might want to learn it. Before you plan what to say, remember the time you didn't know it. What confused you? What finally helped? Let your explanation start there. Then think of one question you could ask them back, something they know that you don't. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once and rest. The bell holds the time.
Oankar close. Guru Nanak's alphabet poem, spoken to a teacher as an invitation: listen, write the Name. Humility for the learned, taught humbly. Today's word.
Your line: humble learning. Today, teach one small thing to someone, starting from where you once got stuck, and ask them one thing back. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-three.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Oankar is Guru Nanak beating a scholar in an argument.
what it means: it's an invitation; its center line says listen, pandit, and points his own letters at the Name.
what a scholar hears: an acrostic on the letters, addressed to a paadha, a teacher of letters; and its singer calls himself lowly in the Japji.
